name: Sewer sequencer
subtitle: a sewer box that reads every virus passing
job: Stop an outbreak in its first week

effects.effect: everything in a sample can be read at once, without knowing what to look for
a strand of bait DNA grabs its matching strand out of a mixture
a single molecule threaded through a tiny hole changes the current letter by letter

how: A new pathogen is usually found weeks after it starts spreading, because a doctor has to suspect something and order a test for it. A box plumbed into a city sewer or an airport terminal's waste line skims the solids out of the flow and sequences everything in them, pulling rare genetic material forward with bait strands that grab anything resembling a virus; a model then flags sequences that match nothing known but are rising week on week. Because it looks for no particular germ, it can see the one nobody has named yet.
obstacle: Pathogen genetic material is a vanishingly small fraction of sewage, so catching a rare new virus at low prevalence still costs a lot of sequencing per site.
evidence: Toronto Pearson airport aircraft and terminal wastewater sequencing detected novel SARS-CoV-2 lineages 1-4 weeks (once 16 weeks) before clinical detection, Scientific Reports 2024, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39489759/ ; cost and sensitivity modelled by the Nucleic Acid Observatory, who show hybridization capture sharply raises sensitivity, https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2023.12.22.23300450v1.full
existsCheck: Searched airport/aircraft wastewater surveillance and untargeted air and sewage metagenomics 2024-2025. Deployed systems (CDC's JFK programme, Canadian airports) run targeted PCR plus variant sequencing of one known virus; pathogen-agnostic detection of an unknown germ is described in every source as a future possibility, not a demonstrated result. No continuous in-sewer sequencer product exists.
tenX: Time from first human infection to naming the pathogen: weeks or months down to days, and it covers unknown germs rather than one on a test panel
why: The first instrument that watches for diseases nobody has named yet, the way seismographs watch for earthquakes.

name: Air germ catcher
subtitle: a ceiling box that names what is spreading
job: Stop an outbreak in its first week

effects.effect: a sharp charged point throws a wind of ions that sweeps dust and droplets out of the air
a high-voltage point quietly charges the air around it
a guided enzyme cuts DNA at any spot spelled out by a short RNA

how: A school or a ward only learns that something is going around once children and patients are already sick, and swabbing everyone is far too slow and expensive. A box on the ceiling runs a needle at high voltage, which charges the air and drives a steady breeze that sweeps airborne droplets onto a collecting plate the size of a stamp, with no fan and no filter to change. Every night the plate is wetted, which wakes up freeze-dried reactions that copy any genetic material present and let guided cutting enzymes release a visible signal for each germ on the list, while the rest of the sample is kept for sequencing if the signal is new.
obstacle: Viruses in room air are extremely dilute, so the collector has to concentrate hours of air into a droplet without destroying the fragile genetic material it is trying to read.
evidence: Nguyen et al., Nature Biotechnology 2021: freeze-dried cell-free CRISPR (SHERLOCK) sensors embedded in a face mask detected SARS-CoV-2 from a wearer's breath in about 90 minutes at room temperature, with accuracy the authors compare to RT-PCR, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-021-00950-3
existsCheck: Searched wearable and room-air pathogen sensors and air metagenomics 2024-2025. The Wyss mask stayed a proof of concept; deployed building air sampling (hospital studies, aircraft HEPA filters) ships samples to a lab, and published studies report airborne human virus abundance as extremely low. No ceiling unit that collects electrostatically and reports the same night is on the market.
tenX: Detection delay in a building: from a week of clinical cases to one night, at the cost of a smoke detector rather than a laboratory
why: Made buildings able to say what was going around, the way smoke detectors made them able to say fire.

name: Vaccine patch printer
subtitle: a tabletop printer that makes vaccine patches
job: Stop an outbreak in its first week

effects.effect: a dissolving needle shorter than a grain of sand puts a dose in the skin painlessly
a sugar glass holds fragile molecules intact at room temperature
a learned model predicts a protein's 3D shape from its sequence

how: Even when a vaccine is designed in days, it reaches people in months, because filling vials, freezing them and trucking them in cold boxes is the slow part. This machine takes the genetic sequence over the network and prints patches instead: an arm squirts an ink of the vaccine's genetic instructions wrapped in fat droplets and mixed with a dissolving polymer into a mould of hundreds of microscopic needles, and a vacuum underneath pulls the ink down into the tips. The patch dries into a glassy film that sits in a drawer at room temperature and is pressed on an arm by anyone, with no needle, no fridge and no nurse.
obstacle: Throughput: the first printer made 100 patches in two days, so the design has to get thousands of times faster before it can vaccinate a town.
evidence: vander Straeten et al., Nature Biotechnology 42:510-517 (2024, online 2023): a tabletop microneedle vaccine printer; patches shelf-stable at least 6 months at room temperature, immune response in mice comparable to intramuscular injection, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-023-01774-z
existsCheck: Searched microneedle vaccine patch manufacture and printers. Microneedle flu and measles patches are in human trials, but they are factory-made; the printer itself is preclinical (mice and pig skin) and no deployable unit exists. The deck's existing cards cover vaccine storage (glass-dried vaccine pack, solar vaccine fridge), not manufacture at the outbreak.
tenX: Weeks from sequence to doses in arms rather than months, and no cold chain at all
why: Turned vaccine supply from a factory and a cold chain into a file sent to a printer.

name: Virus-family vaccine
subtitle: one shot against a whole family of viruses
job: Stop an outbreak in its first week

effects.effect: a ball studded with eight different relatives' proteins trains the immune system only on the parts they share
designed proteins snap themselves together into a regular cage
the body learns to fight a germ

how: Designing a vaccine against a brand-new virus takes months we do not have, so the only way to be ready in week one is to have the vaccine already made. On a protein cage the width of a virus, the grabbing parts of eight different relatives from the same family are planted in a random mosaic, so an immune cell that reaches across two neighbours can only bind where all eight look alike, which is exactly the part a new relative will share. The result is a shot made and stockpiled years before the outbreak, protecting against a virus that had not yet infected anyone when the vial was filled.
obstacle: Proving it works against a virus that does not exist yet: regulators have no accepted way to license a vaccine whose target has not appeared.
evidence: Cohen et al., Science 2022 (mosaic-8): nanoparticles displaying eight sarbecovirus receptor-binding domains protected mice and macaques against SARS-CoV and animal sarbecoviruses absent from the vaccine, where a single-strain vaccine protected only against its own strain, https://authors.library.caltech.edu/records/naz36-42m36 ; follow-up mosaic-7COM in Cell, 2025
existsCheck: Searched mosaic nanoparticle and broadly protective coronavirus and flu vaccines 2022-2026. Mosaic-8b and mosaic-7COM remain in animal studies and early trials; licensed vaccines (including the deck's mRNA vaccine card) all target one named strain. No pre-outbreak family vaccine is approved or stockpiled.
tenX: Vaccine lead time against a brand-new pathogen: from months to zero, because it is already in the freezer
why: Pre-empted pandemics by vaccinating against virus families instead of chasing each new strain.

name: Wall-socket MRI
subtitle: a whole-body scanner that plugs into a socket

effects.effect: atomic resonance
a learned model pulls a clean image out of signals swamped by electrical noise
a weak magnet needs no shielded room and no liquid helium

how: Most cancers are found once they cause symptoms, because the scan that would have seen them early costs millions to install, needs a shielded room and a helium supply, and is rationed. This scanner uses a magnet a sixtieth the usual strength, so it runs off an ordinary wall socket, needs no cage around it and cannot pull metal across the room; the faint, noisy signal is cleaned up by a model trained on strong-magnet images, which learns to tell the body's echo from the hum of the building. A scan then costs about what a blood test costs, which is what makes scanning healthy people worth doing at all.
obstacle: Proving that the learned images are trustworthy for finding small tumours, not just recognisable, since the model has to be believed where no strong-magnet scan exists to check it against.
evidence: Zhao, Ding, Lau, Wu et al., Science 384:eadm7168 (10 May 2024): whole-body imaging at 0.05 T with no radiofrequency or magnetic shielding, about 1,800 W from a wall outlet, 30 volunteers, deep-learning reconstruction; authors estimate roughly $22,000 of hardware at scale, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11496770/
existsCheck: Searched low-field and portable MRI products. Hyperfine's Swoop is a commercial 0.064 T scanner, but it is head-only and for bedside stroke imaging, not whole-body screening; the Hong Kong 0.05 T whole-body system is a research prototype and a Science perspective notes low-field MRI needs more work before wide clinical use. Nothing is marketed for routine whole-body cancer screening.
tenX: Cost per whole-body scan and per installed scanner falls roughly fifty-fold, which is what makes screening healthy people affordable
why: Made the scan cheap enough to give everyone, so cancer was usually found at stage one.

name: Tumour-finding probiotic
subtitle: a drink that makes tumours show in urine

effects.effect: harmless gut bacteria multiply inside a tumour and nowhere else in the body
catalysis
a guided enzyme cuts DNA at any spot spelled out by a short RNA

how: A tumour the size of a pinhead sheds far too little into the blood to find, so cancers are caught years later than they start. A swallowed dose of an ordinary probiotic bacterium, engineered to carry a marker-making enzyme, is cleared from healthy tissue by the immune system but survives and multiplies a millionfold in the oxygen-starved, immune-blind inside of a tumour; the enzyme cuts a harmless substance the patient also swallows, releasing a fragment that leaves in the urine. The tumour therefore amplifies its own signal, and a paper strip dipped in the sample shows a line.
obstacle: Safety and regulation: deliberately giving live engineered bacteria to healthy people for screening is a much higher bar than giving them to someone already ill.
evidence: Danino et al., Science Translational Medicine 2015: orally delivered E. coli Nissle 1917 carrying a lacZ reporter colonised about 90% of liver metastases in mice (10^6-fold enrichment, tumours above ~1 mm^3) with no colonisation of healthy or fibrotic liver, giving a urine signal within 24 h from 1 microlitre, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4511399/ ; paper-strip CRISPR readout of urine barcodes, Hao et al., Nature Nanotechnology 2023
existsCheck: Searched engineered probiotic diagnostics and urinary cancer tests. Blood tests on sale (Galleri) report only about 40% overall sensitivity and were not designed for stage I; engineered bacteria for cancer are in trials as therapy, not as a screening test, and the probiotic reporter work remains in mice. The deck's nearest cards (Gut Diary, Sugar-sensing toilet, Breath screening card) read chemistry the body already makes, not a signal the tumour is made to amplify.
tenX: Smallest detectable tumour drops from roughly a centimetre to a millimetre, a thousandfold in volume, from a drink and a paper strip
why: Let a tumour the size of a pinhead announce itself, using bacteria as the amplifier.

name: Vein magnet
subtitle: a vein wire that catches cancer cells

effects.effect: a steep magnetic field gradient drags magnetically tagged cells sideways out of flowing blood
an antibody binds only its own target
magnetoresistance

how: An early tumour sheds perhaps one cell into a litre of blood, so the usual teaspoon drawn into a tube almost always misses it, and that is why blood tests find cancer late. A thin wire strung with magnets is slipped into an arm vein through an ordinary drip line, after an injection of magnetic particles coated with antibodies that stick to tumour cells; over an hour the patient's whole blood volume washes past the wire many times and the field gradient plucks the tagged cells onto it. Pulling the wire out gives the laboratory the catch from litres of blood instead of millilitres.
obstacle: Getting the injected magnetic particles approved for healthy people, and making them stick to tumour cells of every kind rather than a few known types.
evidence: Vermesh, Gambhir et al., Nature Biomedical Engineering 2018 (MagWIRE): a magnetic wire placed through a standard IV catheter captured 10-80x more tumour cells than a 5 ml blood draw in pigs, with 56% capture of pre-labelled cells in whole blood, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6261517
existsCheck: Searched intravascular tumour cell capture and circulating tumour cell devices. CellSearch and similar systems still process a drawn tube of blood; apheresis-based capture is experimental; MagWIRE has only been used in pigs and would need approval for its nanoparticles. No in-vein capture device is in clinical use.
tenX: Blood volume searched per test rises from about 5 millilitres to several litres, a thousandfold, raising the odds of catching a stage-one tumour's one shed cell
why: Searched the whole bloodstream instead of a teaspoon of it, making one shed cell findable.

name: Decoy node
subtitle: an implant that catches the first spreading cells

effects.effect: a porous implant recruits immune cells, and travelling tumour cells follow them and settle
small particles scatter light
the body rejects foreign tissue

how: What kills in cancer is the spread, and spread is found only once it has built tumours in the liver, lung or brain, by which time it is too late to cure. A sugar-cube of porous polymer implanted under the skin is colonised by the patient's own immune cells, which makes it look to a wandering tumour cell exactly like the soft, welcoming niche it is hunting for, so the first escaping cells lodge there instead of in an organ. A light beam played over the skin reads the fine structure inside the implant and shows when something has moved in, and the whole cube can be lifted out under local anaesthetic to say what it is.
obstacle: Scaling from mice to people: a cube that catches a useful share of travelling cells in a human bloodstream may have to be far larger, or there may have to be several.
evidence: Azarin, Shea et al., Nature Communications 2015: porous poly(caprolactone) scaffolds implanted in mice captured metastatic breast cancer cells before tumours appeared in lung or liver, read label-free by inverse spectroscopic optical coherence tomography, and removing the primary tumour after a scaffold-positive result improved survival, https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms9094 ; follow-up in Cancer Research reported 64% fewer cancer cells in liver and 75% fewer in brain in scaffold-bearing mice
existsCheck: Searched implantable metastasis traps and sentinel scaffolds. The Michigan/Northwestern group states it is still developing a clinical trial protocol; nothing is implanted in patients, and all published work is in mice. The deck's Breathing Scaffold is a scaffold that feeds growing tissue oxygen, a different job.
tenX: Spread is caught at the first escaped cells rather than at a visible organ tumour, moving detection from stage four to months before stage two
why: Gave cancer somewhere harmless to spread to, and so an alarm before it reached an organ.

name: Light-echo breast scanner
subtitle: a laser maps the vessels a tumour grows

effects.effect: a flash of light absorbed in tissue makes it expand and thump out an ultrasound pulse
hemoglobin carries oxygen in the blood
sound echoes

how: Mammograms squash the breast, use X-rays and miss much of what is there in dense tissue, which is why young women are not screened and why tumours are found late in exactly the people whose cancers grow fastest. A bowl of listening crystals surrounds the breast while a near-infrared laser pulses into it; blood soaks up the light far more strongly than the tissue around it, heats by a thousandth of a degree, expands and thumps out a faint ultrasound ping, so the detectors hear a map of every vessel. A tumour only millimetres across has already grown its own tangle of crooked new vessels, and that tangle is what shows up, in a scan that takes seconds, needs no X-rays and no compression.
obstacle: Depth: light reaches a few centimetres into tissue, so the method suits the breast and the skin but cannot yet look deep inside the body.
evidence: Lin et al., Nature Communications 2018: single-breath-hold photoacoustic computed tomography imaged human breast vasculature and identified a tumour missed by angiographic imaging, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6003984/ ; a 2025 dual photoacoustic-ultrasonic system reports whole-breast scans in 12 seconds to 5 cm depth, and Tong et al., Nature Biomedical Engineering 2025, classify lesions with panoramic PACT
existsCheck: Searched photoacoustic breast imaging and screening. Systems are research prototypes or early clinical studies for characterising known lesions; no photoacoustic scanner is approved for population screening, and reviews frame small early-stage lesions as the open gap. The deck's Raman cancer probe reads chemistry in an open surgical field, not vessels through intact tissue.
tenX: Screening becomes safe to repeat often and works in dense breasts, where mammography misses roughly a third of cancers
why: Found tumours by the new blood vessels they build, with light and sound instead of X-rays.

name: Organ bank
subtitle: donor organs turned to glass for years

effects.effect: a strong enough cryoprotectant cooled fast enough sets as glass, with no ice crystals to tear cells
iron particles in an alternating magnetic field heat from within, warming a whole organ evenly in seconds
supercooling

how: A donated kidney is only good for about a day, so organs are flown out within hours to whoever is reachable rather than whoever matches best, and thousands are thrown away each year for want of a recipient in time. The organ is perfused with a cryoprotectant that sets as glass instead of ice, laced with iron oxide particles, and cooled to about minus 150 degrees; to bring it back, the whole organ is put in an alternating magnetic field, and the particles spread through every vessel heat it from the inside fast enough that ice never has time to form. With a bank, matching stops being a race against the clock, organs can be tissue-matched properly, and transplants become scheduled operations.
obstacle: Scale: a human kidney is hundreds of times the volume of a rat's, so getting cryoprotectant everywhere and cooling without cracking is still unsolved.
evidence: Han, Rao, Bischof et al., Nature Communications 14 (June 2023): rat kidneys vitrified and stored up to 100 days, nanowarmed and transplanted, restoring life-sustaining function in all five recipients within 30 days, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-38824-8 ; in October 2026 the same group reported pig kidneys stored for up to a year, rewarmed and transplanted, https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/10/15/1146091/pig-kidneys-that-were-frozen-for-a-year-have-been-brought-back-to-life
existsCheck: Searched organ cryopreservation and organ banking status 2025-2026. No human organ has been vitrified and transplanted; the Minnesota method is licensable but at the rat and pig stage, and the authors' own preprint lists cooling, cryoprotectant toxicity and transport as open problems. Clinical practice is cold storage or normothermic machine perfusion, both measured in hours.
tenX: Shelf life from about 24 hours to a year, which both ends organ discard and lets every transplant be properly matched
why: Turned transplantation from a race against a clock into a bank, the way blood banking changed surgery.

name: Organ reviver
subtitle: restarts organs an hour after the heart stops

effects.effect: a cell-free fluid carrying anti-inflammatory and anti-cell-death compounds halts the cascade that kills starved tissue
pulsed rather than steady flow reopens vessels that have collapsed and clotted
hemoglobin carries oxygen in the blood

how: Almost all organs are lost not for want of donors but because only a tiny fraction of deaths happen where circulation can be kept going; everywhere else the organs are written off within minutes. This machine, a heart-lung bypass pump driving a synthetic cell-free fluid rather than blood, is connected after the heart has been stopped for an hour: the fluid is pulsed through at pressures that force open collapsed vessels, and it carries compounds that block the self-destruct cascade starved cells begin, so circulation is restored throughout the body and kidneys, liver and heart recover function. If organs can be recovered an hour after death rather than in the first minutes, the donor pool stops being the limit.
obstacle: It works on the whole body, including the brain, so it cannot be used without first settling in law and in medicine what it means that a declared-dead body has circulation again.
evidence: Andrijevic, Vrselja, Sestan et al., Nature 608:405 (August 2022, OrganEx): after 1 hour of warm whole-body ischaemia in pigs, pulsatile perfusion with a cytoprotective cell-free perfusate preserved tissue integrity, cut cell death and restored molecular and cellular function across vital organs, with electrical activity and contraction in the heart, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35922506/
existsCheck: Searched organ recovery after circulatory death and normothermic regional perfusion. Clinical practice (NRP, TransMedics OCS) starts within minutes and perfuses with blood; OrganEx is a research system used only in pigs and its own authors call for oversight before any further work. No device recovers organs an hour after death.
tenX: The share of deaths that can yield transplantable organs rises from a couple of percent towards most of them, a ten-to-fiftyfold increase in supply
why: Showed organ death is a cascade that can be stopped, and multiplied the donor pool many times over.

name: Lymph-node liver
subtitle: spare livers grown in your own lymph nodes

effects.effect: a lymph node's rich blood supply and open mesh let injected organ cells organise into working tissue
cells live outside the body
the liver stores sugar as glycogen and releases it

how: A failing liver needs a whole donated organ and a major operation, so most people with end-stage liver disease simply wait and die. Liver cells from one donor are injected through a fine needle into a handful of the patient's own lymph nodes, which already have the plumbing and the open structure an organ needs: the cells engraft there, grow their own blood supply and mature into small working livers, several at once, doing the real job of filtering and making proteins. One donated liver can seed dozens of patients, and the procedure is an endoscopic injection instead of a transplant.
obstacle: Dose and durability: it is not yet shown in people that enough liver tissue grows, or lasts long enough, to replace a failing organ rather than merely help it.
evidence: LyGenesis Phase 2a (NCT04496479) in end-stage liver disease at Houston Methodist and Tufts: in March 2025 the Data and Safety Monitoring Board reviewed the first cohort of four patients and cleared dose escalation, with safety and tolerability reported as encouraging, https://www.biospace.com/press-releases/data-and-safety-monitoring-board-approves-lygenesiss-phase-2a-clinical-trial-to-continue-and-dose-escalate-in-novel-trial-of-organ-regeneration
existsCheck: Searched ectopic organ regeneration and LyGenesis results 2025. Only interim safety news exists, no efficacy results; no approved therapy grows an organ in a lymph node, and hepatocyte transplantation into the liver or spleen, which is tried clinically, engrafts poorly. Nothing in the deck grows an organ in an existing body site.
tenX: One donor organ treats dozens of patients instead of one, and a transplant becomes an injection
why: Found spare building sites for organs already inside the body, so one donor served dozens.

name: Machine-edited donor organ
subtitle: edited on the pump so nobody rejects it

effects.effect: a vector flushed through an organ's own vessels reaches every cell in it, which is impossible inside a patient
double-stranded RNA silences the matching gene
the body rejects foreign tissue

how: A transplant costs the recipient a lifetime of drugs that hold the immune system down, which brings infections and cancers, and the graft is still slowly destroyed; this is why organs are given sparingly and only to those sick enough to be worth the trade. While a donated organ sits on the perfusion pump, warm and beating, it is a closed system with its own plumbing, so gene-carrying vectors pumped into it reach every cell: they switch off the surface markers by which a stranger's immune system recognises the organ as foreign, and blunt the inflammation that follows the operation. The organ is edited before it is ever connected to a patient, so no drug has to hold the patient's immune system down.
obstacle: An organ hidden from the immune system is also hidden from the defences that watch for infected and cancerous cells in it, and the editing has to be complete enough to matter without being permanent elsewhere.
evidence: Figueiredo et al., Frontiers in Immunology 2020: lentiviral vectors delivered during sub-normothermic machine perfusion silenced beta-2-microglobulin and CIITA in rat kidneys with no added cell death, https://frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2020.00265/pdf ; a Human Gene Therapy paper (June 2024) demonstrated CRISPR editing in human lungs on ex vivo perfusion as groundwork for a first-in-human organ study
existsCheck: Searched ex vivo organ gene editing and hypoimmune transplants 2024-2026. All whole-organ work is preclinical or platform-building; hypoimmune editing that has reached patients is in cells (islets, CAR-T), not organs, and every transplant today still requires immunosuppression. The deck's Pig kidney with a human lining relines vessels with cells, rather than editing the organ's own genes on the pump.
tenX: Lifelong immunosuppression removed and graft survival roughly doubled, which widens who can be transplanted at all
why: Used the hours an organ spends on a pump to make it immune-invisible, ending immunosuppression.

name: Pig-grown human kidney
subtitle: a pig embryo grows a patient's own kidney

effects.effect: some embryo cells steer how their neighbours develop
an embryo with its kidney genes switched off leaves an empty niche that foreign stem cells fill
four genes turn an adult cell back into a stem cell that can become any tissue

how: There is no way to grow an organ in a dish, because nothing we build supplies the blood and the months of development an organ needs. A pig embryo has both, so two of its kidney-building genes are switched off, leaving a vacancy, and stem cells made from the patient's own skin are injected to fill it; the embryo's own signals then direct those human cells through the whole programme of kidney development while the sow carries it. The organ that grows is built from the patient's cells, so it needs no immunosuppression, and it is grown to order rather than waited for.
obstacle: Human cells are badly outcompeted in a pig embryo, so far only to day 28 and only to an early kidney stage, and letting such a pregnancy go to term raises ethical questions nobody has settled.
evidence: Wang, Dai, Pan, Lai et al., Cell Stem Cell (7 September 2023): human iPSCs with MYCN and BCL2 support generated humanized mesonephros with tubules in pig embryos to day 28, from 1,820 transferred embryos and 13 surrogates, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37683604/
existsCheck: Searched interspecies chimera organogenesis and xenotransplantation 2023-2026. Xenotransplants now reaching patients use gene-edited pig organs made of pig cells, which still need heavy immunosuppression; humanized chimeric organs have never gone past early embryonic stages. The deck's Pig kidney with a human lining is a pig organ relined with human cells, not an organ grown from the patient's own cells.
tenX: An organ on demand for anyone, made of their own cells, instead of a waiting list and a lifetime of drugs
why: Borrowed a pig embryo's development to grow organs from a patient's own cells.

name: Dancing-molecule gel
subtitle: an injected gel nerves grow through
job: Repair the brain and spinal cord

effects.effect: how fast molecules jiggle within an assembly sets how strongly they can signal a cell's receptors
viscoelasticity
a plant hormone drives growth

how: A cut in the spinal cord seals itself with scar tissue, and central nerves will not grow through it, which is why paralysis is permanent. A liquid injected into the injury self-assembles into a mesh of nanofibres carrying two signals copied from the body's own growth cues, and the trick is that the molecules in the mesh are deliberately left loosely bound, so they move about rapidly; receptors on nerve cells are themselves in motion, and signals that keep up with them are read far more strongly than signals held rigidly in place. In mice, one injection a day after a severe injury restored walking.
obstacle: It has worked in rodents and in injured human spinal cord grown in a dish, but no human has been treated yet.
evidence: Alvarez, Stupp et al., Science 2021: a single injection of a supramolecular scaffold with fast-moving molecules 24 hours after severe spinal cord injury restored walking in mice, with slow-moving versions far less effective; FDA Orphan Drug Designation July 2025; Northwestern's February 2026 Nature Biomedical Engineering paper reports the same therapy driving neurite outgrowth in injured human spinal cord organoids containing microglia, https://news.northwestern.edu/stories/2026/02/paralysis-treatment-heals-lab-grown-human-spinal-cord-organoids
existsCheck: Searched spinal cord injury therapies in trials 2025-2026. Nothing restores central nerve growth in people; approved care is surgical stabilisation and rehabilitation, and Amphix Bio is only targeting late 2026 for first trials. The deck's nerve cards (Self-sealing brain implant coating, Rechargeable numbing implant) do not regrow nerves.
tenX: Function recovered after a complete injury rather than none, and from one injection instead of no option at all
why: Showed that how fast a molecule moves, not just its shape, decides whether a nerve regrows.

name: Guided nerve regrowth
subtitle: nerves regrown and steered to their old targets
job: Repair the brain and spinal cord

effects.effect: a regrown axon only restores function if it is steered to the exact region it used to serve
a cell follows genes put into it
chemical attractants laid in a gradient pull a growing nerve tip along them

how: Decades of work got nerves to regrow across spinal injuries without restoring any movement, and the reason turned out to be that the regrown fibres wander and connect to the wrong places. Single-cell sequencing is used to pick out which few neuron types actually matter for walking; a gene-carrying virus is then injected to switch their growth programmes back on, while a trail of attractant proteins is laid from the injury down to the exact segment of the cord those fibres used to serve, so the regrowing tips follow it home. Mice with anatomically complete injuries walked again, with a gait like that of animals recovering from partial injuries.
obstacle: The chemical trail has to be laid over the length of a human spinal cord, centimetres rather than millimetres, and held in place for the months that regrowth takes.
evidence: Squair, Anderson, Courtine et al., Science (22 September 2023): chemoattracting and guiding the transected axons of identified neuron subpopulations to their natural target region restored walking after complete spinal cord injury in mice, whereas regrowth without guidance did not, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37733871/
existsCheck: Searched spinal cord gene therapy and axon guidance 2023-2026. All of it is rodent work and the authors say many obstacles remain before human use; no gene therapy for spinal cord injury is approved or in registrational trials. No existing card or product guides regrown fibres to a target region.
tenX: Walking recovered after an anatomically complete injury, where regrowth alone gives essentially nothing
why: Proved regrowth is not enough: nerves must be addressed to their old targets, and then showed how.

name: Grafted neuron bridge
subtitle: an implant that grows its own nerve wiring
job: Repair the brain and spinal cord

effects.effect: neurons grown on an implant send their own axons into the host and make the connections metal cannot
light-sensitive proteins let a flash of light switch chosen nerve cells on or off
electrodes on the motor cortex let a person's intent move a cursor or arm

how: An electrode is a blunt instrument: it is a thousand times bigger than a nerve cell, it scars, and it can only shout at whole neighbourhoods of neurons at once, which is why implants give coarse control and fade over years. This implant instead carries a living layer of lab-grown neurons on its face; placed on the brain or either side of a spinal injury, those cells send their own axons out into the tissue and form real synapses, so the device talks to the nervous system in its own language. The implant drives its grafted cells with flashes of light and reads them back optically, keeping the metal outside the body's own circuitry.
obstacle: Keeping grafted neurons alive and wired for years, and showing they connect reliably: in the first mouse test only five of nine animals learned the light-cued task.
evidence: Science Corporation's biohybrid interface: a grid holding a layer of stem-cell-derived neurons on the mouse cortex, where light delivered to the grafted cells drove a learned behaviour in 5 of 9 mice, https://spectrum.ieee.org/brain-computer-interface-2671151260 ; Rochford et al., Science Advances 2023 report a biohybrid regenerative interface restoring function in severed rat peripheral nerve, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10032597/
existsCheck: Searched biohybrid neural interfaces 2023-2026. Every clinical brain-computer interface (Utah arrays, Neuralink, Blackrock, Synchron) is metal or polymer electrodes in direct contact with tissue; biohybrid devices with living neurons are in rodents only, and the groups themselves name human cells as the next milestone. No existing card bridges a nerve with grafted cells.
tenX: Connections per implant go from thousands of electrode contacts to the neuron-by-neuron synapses a graft makes, and the interface stops degrading as scar builds
why: Stopped trying to wire metal into the brain and let living neurons make the connections instead.

name: Nerve dust
subtitle: hundreds of dust-sized chips bridge a cut cord
job: Repair the brain and spinal cord

effects.effect: a chip smaller than a grain of salt harvests the power it needs from a radio field
each grain answers on its own address, so one radio patch coordinates hundreds of them
electrodes on the motor cortex let a person's intent move a cursor or arm

how: Bridging a spinal injury at a useful bandwidth means listening to and speaking with thousands of nerve cells at once, and today that means thick wire bundles through the skull or spine, which scar, break and leak. Instead, hundreds of chips a quarter of a millimetre across are sprinkled across the cord or cortex, each with no battery and no wire: a patch worn on the skin floods them with radio power, and each grain has its own network address, so the patch polls them one by one the way a cell tower handles phones. Signals read above the injury can then be played back into the grains below it, bridging the gap in both directions.
obstacle: Power and bandwidth per grain are tiny, and nobody has yet shown hundreds of them working in a human for years without the brain's defences walling them off.
evidence: Lee, Leung, Nurmikko et al., Nature Electronics 4:604-614 (12 August 2021): 48 untethered 0.25 mm^2 neurograins, powered and addressed by an external skin-patch radio, recorded spontaneous cortical activity in a rat, with the design supporting up to about 770, https://dx.doi.org/10.1038/s41928-021-00631-8
existsCheck: Searched wireless microscale neural implants 2021-2026. Clinical systems all use tethered arrays or a single implanted can (Utah array, Neuralink, Synchron, Stentrode); neurograins and similar neural dust remain rodent demonstrations, limited to 48 units by the animal's brain size. No existing card distributes an implant into independent wireless grains.
tenX: Channels bridging an injury rise from a few hundred wired contacts towards tens of thousands, with no cable through the skin
why: Replaced the cable into the nervous system with a cloud of radio-powered grains.

name: Electric-field spine patch
subtitle: a daily electric field guides nerve growth
job: Repair the brain and spinal cord

effects.effect: a growing nerve tip turns and grows towards the negative pole of a weak electric field
an oxide film holds and releases charge at its surface instead of corroding like bare metal
muscles work by electrical impulses

how: A damaged spinal cord is not only scarred, it has lost the faint electrical field that guided its nerves as they grew in the embryo, and a nerve tip with nothing to steer by does not cross the gap. A flexible film slipped under the cord's outer membrane holds two charge-storing oxide electrodes that apply a weak direct field across the injury for an hour a day; growing tips turn towards the negative side, so the field acts as a compass across the scar, and the same field also calms the dying-back of cells around the wound. Because the electrodes store charge in an oxide surface rather than passing current through bare metal, they neither corrode nor inflame the cord.
obstacle: In rats the benefit looked protective rather than regenerative, with axon density unchanged at twelve weeks, so it is not yet clear the field really guides new growth.
evidence: Harland, Matter et al., Nature Communications 16:5372 (June 2025): a thin-film implant with sputtered iridium oxide supercapacitive electrodes placed under the dura delivered a daily electric field after thoracic contusion injury in rats, improving locomotion and coordination from week 4 with no neuroinflammatory response, https://research.chalmers.se/en/publication/547408
existsCheck: Searched electric field therapy for spinal cord injury 2025. Earlier human attempts (oscillating field stimulators) used corroding metal electrodes outside the dura and were abandoned; this implant is in rats, with dose-finding the stated next step. Epidural stimulators now in patients drive muscles below an injury rather than steering nerve growth.
tenX: An implant the thickness of a film, with no drug and no cells, moves a complete-injury animal from no recovery to measurable walking
why: Revived the embryo's electrical compass for nerve growth, in a film that does not corrode.
